items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Aluminium 'should' fizz in water — why does it sit on the kitchen worktop?
items.claim: Aluminium is above iron, zinc and tin in the reactivity series. By the textbook, it should corrode rapidly. Yet aluminium foil, cans, ladders and aircraft hulls last for years.
items.prompt: Why is aluminium so unreactive in practice?

options.text: Pure aluminium does not react with oxygen
Aluminium reacts instantly with air to form a coherent, impermeable 4-nanometre layer of Al2O3 that protects the metal beneath; the reactive metal is locked behind its own oxide
Aluminium is coated with plastic at the factory
The reactivity series is wrong about aluminium

items.reveal:
Aluminium oxide forms in milliseconds when fresh aluminium meets air. Unlike iron oxide, Al2O3 has nearly the same molar volume as the metal it formed from (Pilling-Bedworth ratio about 1.3). The result is a tight, adherent film that excludes further oxygen.

Scratch the surface and a new film forms instantly. Dissolve the film in strong alkali (NaOH) or amalgamate the surface with mercury and the bare metal reacts violently — aluminium powder mixed with iron oxide is thermite, used for welding rails.

Anodising — deliberately growing a thicker oxide film electrochemically — gives extra protection and a surface that can hold dyes.
items.why: Reactivity series describes thermodynamic tendency. Passivation is the kinetic gatekeeper that decides whether reactions actually happen.

items.title: Scale up an atom and the nucleus would be a fly in a cathedral
items.claim: An atom is roughly 10 to the minus 10 m across. Its nucleus is around 10 to the minus 15 m. Scale a hydrogen atom up to the size of St Paul's Cathedral dome (about 30 m across) and the nucleus would be the size of a housefly hovering at the centre.

options.text: Almost nothing — the electron is a smeared probability cloud over an enormous volume; the rest of the atom is empty space pervaded by the electron's wavefunction

items.reveal:
The volume ratio between atom and nucleus is about 10 to the 15. Pack a marble-sized nucleus and the surrounding atom is a sphere about 1 km across.

Rutherford's gold foil result (1909): alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly pass through with little deflection. About 1 in 8000 bounce back. Only a tiny central charge can produce that — the plum pudding model is wrong, the nucleus is born.

Solidity comes from electromagnetic repulsion between electron clouds and from the Pauli exclusion principle, not from atoms physically touching. Walls are mostly nothing — they just resist intrusion of one electron cloud into another.
items.why: Students picture atoms as little balls. They are tiny dense cores surrounded by enormous fields of probability.
